title: Pediatric Neurosurgery & Hydrocephalus
summary: Operating on the developing nervous system.

lessons.title: Hydrocephalus: Shunts & ETV

levels.kid:
Your brain floats in a clear liquid called **CSF**. It is like water in a fish tank that is always being made and always draining away.

Sometimes the drain gets blocked. The liquid builds up inside the brain's little rooms, called **ventricles**, and they get too big. That is **hydrocephalus**, which means "water head." In a baby, the head can grow too fast and the soft spot can bulge.

Doctors fix it two ways. A **shunt** is a thin tube that carries extra liquid to the belly, where the body soaks it up. Or a surgeon makes a tiny new door inside the brain so the liquid can flow around the block. That is called an **ETV**.
levels.hs:
**Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)** is made mostly by the **choroid plexus** inside the ventricles, flows from the lateral ventricles to the third ventricle, through the narrow **cerebral aqueduct** to the fourth ventricle, then out into the space around the brain and spinal cord, where it is absorbed into the venous system. An adult makes roughly half a liter a day, so it is replaced several times daily.

**Hydrocephalus** happens when CSF builds up and the ventricles enlarge.
- **Obstructive (non-communicating)**: something blocks flow inside the ventricles, such as **aqueductal stenosis** or a tumor.
- **Communicating**: flow is open, but absorption fails, for example after bleeding or meningitis.

In babies, whose skull sutures are still open, signs include a fast-growing head, a **bulging fontanelle**, irritability, vomiting and **"sunsetting" eyes** that look downward. Older children get headaches, vomiting and sleepiness.

Two main treatments:
- **Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt**: a catheter in the ventricle, a one-way valve, and tubing tunneled under the skin to the abdomen.
- **Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV)**: a camera is passed into the ventricles and a small hole is made in the floor of the third ventricle, letting CSF bypass the blockage.
levels.college:
**Pathophysiology.** Hydrocephalus is an imbalance between CSF production and absorption that enlarges the ventricles, usually with raised intracranial pressure. Classic categories are **obstructive** (block within the ventricular system: aqueductal stenosis, posterior fossa tumors, colloid cyst, Chiari II, Dandy-Walker) and **communicating** (absorption failure at the arachnoid granulations or along venous and lymphatic routes: post-hemorrhagic, post-infectious). Modern models stress that CSF also moves along perivascular spaces and drains partly to lymphatics, so the old "bulk flow only" picture is incomplete.

**Infant presentation.** Because sutures are open, the head enlarges: crossing percentiles on the head-circumference chart, a tense fontanelle, split sutures, scalp vein distension, and downward gaze from pressure on the dorsal midbrain (Parinaud-type signs). **Post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus** in premature infants after intraventricular hemorrhage is a major cause; temporizing devices such as a **ventricular reservoir** or **ventriculosubgaleal shunt** bridge the baby until a permanent solution is possible.

**Shunts.** A VP shunt has three parts: proximal ventricular catheter, valve (fixed-pressure or **programmable**, set magnetically through the skin), and distal catheter. If the abdomen is unsuitable, the distal end goes to the right atrium or pleural space. Shunts are lifesaving but fail often, through **obstruction**, **infection**, disconnection or fracture, and **overdrainage**.

**ETV.** Through a burr hole, an endoscope enters the lateral ventricle, passes the **foramen of Monro** and perforates the thin floor of the third ventricle between the **mammillary bodies** and the **infundibular recess**, in front of the basilar artery. It works best for obstructive hydrocephalus, especially aqueductal stenosis in older children, and avoids lifelong hardware.
levels.phd:
**Beyond bulk flow.** The textbook circuit (choroid plexus secretion, unidirectional flow, arachnoid granulation absorption) explains obstructive hydrocephalus well but struggles with communicating forms. Research has emphasized pulsatile dynamics, the **glymphatic** exchange of CSF and interstitial fluid along perivascular spaces, and meningeal lymphatic drainage. Choroid plexus secretion itself is an active process involving ion transporters (for example the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter NKCC1), which is why post-hemorrhagic and post-infectious hydrocephalus may involve both hypersecretion and impaired clearance, with inflammation (TLR4 and NF-kB signaling) as a driver in animal models.

**Genetics.** Congenital hydrocephalus has genetic contributors: X-linked **L1CAM** mutations cause aqueductal stenosis with adducted thumbs, and many cases involve genes for neural stem cell fate, ciliary function and Wnt signaling. These findings suggest some ventriculomegaly reflects abnormal brain development, not just plumbing, which may explain why diversion alone does not normalize outcome.

**Predicting ETV success.** The **ETV Success Score** combines age (infants under 6 months do worst), etiology (aqueductal stenosis and tectal tumors best; post-infectious worst) and prior shunt. In infants, adding **choroid plexus cauterization (ETV/CPC)**, developed largely in Uganda to avoid shunt dependence where emergency revision was unavailable, raised success rates in selected patients.

**Shunt failure as a chronic disease.** Pediatric shunts fail at high rates, with a large fraction failing in the first year and many needing several revisions over a lifetime. Hydrocephalus networks have shown that standardized protocols for shunt insertion (antibiotic-impregnated catheters, minimized handling, strict skin preparation) lower infection rates. Valve design trials (fixed versus flow-regulating versus anti-siphon) have not found a clear winner, a reminder that engineering intuition must be tested clinically.

**Adult note.** **Normal pressure hydrocephalus** in older adults presents with gait disturbance, cognitive decline and loss of bladder control; selection uses lumbar drainage trials.
levels.expert:
**The child with a shunt and a headache** is the classic pediatric neurosurgery call. Shunt failure can kill, so the threshold to investigate is low. Symptoms are headache, vomiting, lethargy, irritability, a bulging fontanelle in infants, new squint from sixth nerve palsy, and parents saying "this is how he looked last time." Signs of herniation (bradycardia, hypertension, irregular breathing, fixed pupils) mean emergency tapping of the shunt reservoir or an external drain while the operating room is prepared.

**Workup.** Compare imaging with the child's own baseline, since some shunted ventricles barely change size when they fail (**slit ventricle** physiology). Use **rapid-sequence or fast MRI** to avoid repeated CT radiation, a **shunt series** of X-rays for disconnection or fracture, and a **shunt tap** for pressure and CSF culture when infection is possible. Most infections appear within months of surgery, often skin organisms such as coagulase-negative staphylococci; treatment is usually **externalization or removal** with antibiotics, then a new shunt once CSF clears.

**Programmable valves** can be reset by strong magnets, so check the setting after every MRI.

**Choosing ETV versus shunt.** For an older child with aqueductal stenosis, ETV is first-line. Failure tends to be early; late failure is rarer but can be sudden and dangerous. Intraoperative pitfalls: a thick or opaque floor, small foramen of Monro, distorted anatomy, and the **basilar artery** just behind the target. A bleed from the basilar tip is catastrophic, so the perforation is made in the midline, just behind the infundibular recess, with blunt technique and gentle balloon dilation.

**Long view.** Shunted children need lifelong follow-up, education for families about failure signs, and transition to adult services, where too many patients get lost.

keyPoints: Hydrocephalus is CSF buildup that enlarges the ventricles, usually with raised pressure.
Obstructive hydrocephalus blocks flow inside the ventricles; communicating hydrocephalus fails at absorption.
Infant signs: fast head growth, bulging fontanelle, split sutures, sunsetting eyes.
A VP shunt has a ventricular catheter, a one-way valve and tubing to the abdomen.
ETV perforates the third ventricle floor between the mammillary bodies and infundibular recess, in front of the basilar artery.
Shunts fail often (blockage, infection, overdrainage), so failure signs need urgent assessment.

test.q: Which structure makes most of the CSF?
test.explain: The choroid plexus in the ventricles secretes most CSF; arachnoid granulations help absorb it.

test.q: CSF flows from the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle through the:
test.explain: The narrow cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) links the third and fourth ventricles, and narrowing there is a classic cause of hydrocephalus.

test.q: Hydrocephalus after meningitis, where flow paths are open but absorption fails, is called:
test.explain: Communicating means CSF can still reach the subarachnoid space; the problem is absorption.

test.q: Which is a typical sign of hydrocephalus in an infant?
test.explain: Open sutures let the head expand, and the fontanelle becomes tense and bulging; a sunken one suggests dehydration.

test.q: Where does the distal end of a standard VP shunt drain?
test.explain: Ventriculoperitoneal means ventricle to peritoneum, where CSF is absorbed.

test.q: ETV is most likely to succeed in which case?
choices: An older child with aqueductal stenosis
A child with a working shunt and no symptoms
test.explain: ETV bypasses an obstruction; it works best in obstructive causes like aqueductal stenosis, in children beyond infancy.

test.q: Which artery lies just behind the floor of the third ventricle during ETV?
test.explain: The basilar tip sits behind the floor; injuring it is the most feared ETV complication.

test.q: The device that sets how easily CSF flows through a shunt is the ___.
test.explain: The valve controls opening pressure and prevents backflow.

test.q: What does ETV stand for?
test.explain: A camera-guided hole in the third ventricle floor.

test.q: Downward-deviated eyes in an infant with hydrocephalus are called ___ eyes.
test.explain: Pressure on the dorsal midbrain impairs upgaze, so the eyes look down like a setting sun.

test.q: After an MRI, what must be checked in a child with a programmable shunt?
test.explain: Strong magnets can change a programmable valve's setting.

test.q: Which is NOT a common cause of shunt failure?
test.explain: Shunts fail by obstruction, infection, disconnection or fracture, and overdrainage.

kidTest.q: What is the clear liquid around the brain called?
kidTest.explain: CSF means cerebrospinal fluid.

kidTest.q: Hydrocephalus means:
choices: Too much fluid in the brain
kidTest.explain: It is extra fluid that makes the brain's rooms too big.

kidTest.q: A shunt is a:
choices: Thin tube that drains extra fluid
kidTest.explain: It carries fluid away, usually to the belly.

kidTest.q: In a baby with hydrocephalus, the head may:
kidTest.explain: The skull is soft in babies, so it gets bigger.

kidTest.q: The brain's little fluid-filled rooms are called ___.
kidTest.explain: There are four ventricles.

kidTest.q: An ETV makes:
choices: A tiny new door inside the brain
kidTest.explain: It lets fluid flow around the blockage.

advancedTest.q: A 10-year-old shunted for aqueductal stenosis has headache and vomiting, but CT ventricles look identical to baseline. Best next thinking?
choices: Ventricles may not enlarge in failure; consider tap, ICP evaluation or exploration
Normal CT excludes shunt failure; discharge
advancedTest.explain: Stiff, slit-like ventricles may not dilate despite failure; clinical suspicion drives further testing.

advancedTest.q: Which combination gives the HIGHEST ETV Success Score?
choices: Age 3 months, post-hemorrhagic, no prior shunt
Age over 10, aqueductal stenosis, no prior shunt
advancedTest.explain: Older age, a favorable obstructive cause and no prior shunt all raise predicted success.

advancedTest.q: Why was ETV with choroid plexus cauterization developed for infants in low-resource settings?
choices: Because it removes the need for an endoscope
To avoid lifelong shunt dependence where emergency revision is hard to reach
advancedTest.explain: Shunt failure can be fatal without rapid access to neurosurgery; reducing CSF production plus ETV raised shunt-free success in selected infants.

advancedTest.q: X-linked hydrocephalus with aqueductal stenosis and adducted thumbs is linked to mutations in:
advancedTest.explain: L1CAM encodes a neural cell adhesion molecule; FGFR2 and TWIST1 are craniosynostosis genes.

lessons.title: Craniosynostosis

levels.kid:
A baby's skull is not one solid bowl. It is made of several bone plates with soft seams between them, called **sutures**. The seams let the head grow as the brain grows, like a balloon with stretchy stripes.

Sometimes one seam closes too early. That is **craniosynostosis**. The head cannot grow the normal way at that seam, so it grows extra in other directions and gets an unusual shape, like long and narrow.

Surgeons can help. In tiny babies they can open the seam with a small camera and then use a special **helmet** to guide the shape. In older babies they reshape the skull bones in a bigger operation.
levels.hs:
The infant skull has bony plates joined by fibrous **sutures**: the **metopic** (forehead midline), **coronal** (side to side across the top front), **sagittal** (midline top) and **lambdoid** (back). Soft spots where sutures meet are **fontanelles**. Sutures let the skull expand as the brain roughly triples in volume in the first years.

**Craniosynostosis** is the early fusion of one or more sutures. By **Virchow's law**, growth is blocked at right angles to the fused suture and the skull compensates by growing parallel to it.
- **Sagittal** (most common): long, narrow head, called **scaphocephaly**.
- **Metopic**: triangular forehead, called **trigonocephaly**.
- **Unicoronal**: one side of the forehead flattened, with an asymmetric eye socket.
- **Lambdoid** (rare): flattening at the back.

Much more common is **positional plagiocephaly**, a flat spot from lying in one position. It is not fused bone and usually improves with repositioning, tummy time and sometimes a helmet.

Surgery is done to give the brain room and to correct shape. Options include **endoscopic strip craniectomy** with helmet therapy for young infants, or **open cranial vault remodeling** later in the first year.
levels.college:
**Classification.** Craniosynostosis affects roughly 1 in 2,000 to 2,500 births. Most cases are **nonsyndromic** single-suture fusions; **syndromic** cases often involve multiple sutures plus facial, limb or airway features.

**Suture patterns**:
- **Sagittal**: scaphocephaly with frontal bossing and occipital bulleting.
- **Metopic**: trigonocephaly with a midline forehead ridge and **hypotelorism** (eyes close together). Note that the metopic suture normally closes early in infancy, so a mild ridge alone is not disease.
- **Unicoronal**: anterior plagiocephaly with ipsilateral forehead flattening, a raised orbit (**harlequin eye** on X-ray) and the nasal root deviated toward the fused side.
- **Bicoronal**: brachycephaly (short, wide, tall head), common in syndromes.
- **Lambdoid**: posterior plagiocephaly with the ear pulled back and down on the affected side.

**Positional versus lambdoid.** Viewed from above, positional plagiocephaly forms a **parallelogram**, with the ipsilateral ear and forehead pushed forward. Lambdoid synostosis gives a **trapezoid**, with the ear displaced posteriorly and a bony ridge.

**Syndromes and genes.** Crouzon, Apert and Pfeiffer syndromes involve **FGFR2** variants; Muenke syndrome a specific **FGFR3** variant; Saethre-Chotzen **TWIST1**. Apert adds fused fingers and toes. Midface hypoplasia can cause airway obstruction.

**Raised ICP** risk is low in single-suture disease and higher in multisuture and syndromic cases, which may also have hydrocephalus or Chiari malformation.

**Surgical options**:
- **Endoscopic strip craniectomy** (typically under about 3 to 4 months) followed by months of molding helmet therapy.
- **Spring-assisted cranioplasty**.
- **Open cranial vault remodeling** or **fronto-orbital advancement** (often 6 to 12 months).
- Staged midface advancement or **distraction osteogenesis** in syndromic patients.
levels.phd:
**Suture biology.** A suture is an active growth center: osteogenic fronts on each bone edge are separated by a mesenchymal layer that must stay undifferentiated. Patency depends on signaling between the dura and suture mesenchyme, including FGF, BMP, Wnt and TWIST1-regulated pathways. Gain-of-function **FGFR2** variants in Apert syndrome (the recurrent S252W and P253R substitutions in the linker between immunoglobulin-like domains II and III) change ligand specificity and drive premature osteoblast differentiation. **TWIST1** haploinsufficiency in Saethre-Chotzen shifts the boundary between suture mesenchyme and bone. Mouse work identified **Gli1-positive suture stem cells**; their loss causes fusion, and implanting them with a biodegradable gel has restored suture-like function in animals, a possible future alternative to repeated surgery.

**Form follows constraint.** Virchow's law is a first approximation; finite-element models of the growing skull show that compensatory growth also depends on intracranial pressure, brain growth vectors and the skull base, which is why skull base angulation differs in unicoronal synostosis.

**Neurodevelopment.** Children with single-suture synostosis show higher rates of subtle learning and language difficulties than peers. Whether surgery changes this, and whether earlier surgery is better, remains debated because confounding is difficult and randomized trials are rare. Some studies of sagittal synostosis suggest better cognitive scores with earlier or more extensive repair, but the data are observational.

**Comparative outcomes.** Endoscopic and open approaches give similar shape outcomes for sagittal synostosis in many series, with endoscopy reducing blood loss, transfusion and hospital stay but needing helmet adherence. Cross-center comparisons are confounded by selection, so prospective multicenter registries are now the main tool.
levels.expert:
**Clinic first.** Most referrals for an odd head shape are **positional plagiocephaly**, so the first job is careful examination from above and from the front: suture ridging, ear position, forehead and orbit symmetry, fontanelle feel, and head circumference trend. A confident clinical diagnosis of positional flattening needs no CT. When synostosis is suspected, many centers use **low-dose CT with 3D reconstruction** or ultrasound of the suture to limit radiation.

**Timing decides technique.** A family arriving at two months has the option of an **endoscopic strip craniectomy**, which usually means shorter surgery and much less transfusion, but commits them to a molding helmet worn most of the day for months, with regular adjustments. A family arriving at eight months generally needs **open vault remodeling**.

**Blood is the danger.** Infants have a tiny circulating blood volume, and open vault surgery can lose a large share of it. Teams use **tranexamic acid** (an antifibrinolytic), cell salvage, careful scalp incisions, and close communication between surgeon and anesthesiologist about losses. Venous air embolism is a recognized risk with the head raised and venous sinuses exposed.

**Syndromic cases** need a multidisciplinary craniofacial team: airway (obstructive sleep apnea from midface hypoplasia, sometimes tracheostomy), eyes (exposure keratopathy from shallow orbits, papilledema surveillance), hearing, hand surgery, genetics and psychology. Raised ICP can be silent, so serial fundoscopy or optical coherence tomography and head-circumference tracking matter. Posterior vault distraction is often done first to expand intracranial volume.

**Pitfalls**: treating a normal metopic ridge as disease, missing a second fused suture, and operating late for shape when the real issue was raised pressure.

keyPoints: Sutures are fibrous seams that let the infant skull grow with the brain.
Craniosynostosis is premature suture fusion; growth stops at right angles to the fused suture (Virchow's law).
Sagittal synostosis (most common) gives scaphocephaly; metopic gives trigonocephaly.
Positional plagiocephaly is common, not a fusion, and is usually treated without surgery.
Syndromic forms (Apert, Crouzon, Pfeiffer) involve FGFR2; Saethre-Chotzen involves TWIST1.
Young infants can have endoscopic strip craniectomy plus helmet; older infants need open vault remodeling.

test.q: Craniosynostosis is:
choices: A tumor of the skull bone
Too much CSF in the ventricles
Premature fusion of one or more skull sutures
test.explain: The fused seam stops growth in that direction.

test.q: The most common single suture to fuse early is the:
test.explain: Sagittal synostosis is the most common type; lambdoid is the rarest of the major ones.

test.q: A long, narrow head shape from sagittal synostosis is called:
test.explain: Scapho means boat-shaped; growth is blocked side to side so the head grows front to back.

test.q: A triangular forehead suggests fusion of the:
test.explain: Metopic synostosis gives trigonocephaly and often eyes set close together.

test.q: Virchow's law says skull growth is restricted ___ to the fused suture.
test.explain: Growth stops at right angles to the fused suture and compensates parallel to it.

test.q: Viewed from above, positional plagiocephaly typically looks like a:
test.explain: The ear and forehead on the flat side shift forward; lambdoid synostosis gives a trapezoid instead.

test.q: Which gene is involved in Apert and Crouzon syndromes?
test.explain: Gain-of-function FGFR2 variants drive early suture fusion in these syndromes.

test.q: Name the soft spots where infant skull sutures meet.
test.explain: The anterior fontanelle is the largest and closes in toddlerhood.

test.q: Endoscopic strip craniectomy is usually followed by:
test.explain: The helmet guides skull growth after the fused strip is removed.

test.q: Which is the main danger during open cranial vault remodeling in an infant?
test.explain: Infants have small blood volumes, so even moderate bleeding is a large share.

test.q: Unicoronal synostosis raises the orbit on one side, seen on X-ray as the ___ eye sign.
test.explain: The elevated lesser sphenoid wing gives the harlequin appearance.

test.q: Raised intracranial pressure is most likely in:
test.explain: More fused sutures mean less room for brain growth.

kidTest.q: A baby's skull is made of:
kidTest.explain: The seams let the head grow.

kidTest.q: The soft seams are called:
kidTest.explain: Sutures join the skull plates.

kidTest.q: Craniosynostosis happens when a seam:
kidTest.explain: An early-closing seam changes head shape.

kidTest.q: A flat spot from always lying the same way is:
kidTest.explain: Changing position and tummy time often help.

kidTest.q: A special ___ can help shape a baby's head after a small surgery.
kidTest.explain: The helmet guides growth.

kidTest.q: Why do doctors fix craniosynostosis?
choices: To give the brain room and a normal shape
kidTest.explain: The brain needs space to grow.

advancedTest.q: A 4-month-old has right occipital flattening, the right ear pushed forward and right frontal bossing; the head looks like a parallelogram from above. Best management?
choices: Repositioning, tummy time, possibly a helmet; no CT needed
advancedTest.explain: Ear forward plus ipsilateral frontal bossing is positional; lambdoid synostosis pulls the ear back and gives a trapezoid.

advancedTest.q: Apert syndrome's recurrent FGFR2 variants (S252W, P253R) mainly act by:
choices: Changing ligand binding specificity and promoting osteoblast differentiation
advancedTest.explain: These gain-of-function linker variants alter which FGFs bind, pushing suture cells to become bone.

advancedTest.q: Which is the best reason to choose endoscopic over open repair for sagittal synostosis in a 2-month-old?
choices: Less blood loss and transfusion, if the family can manage helmet therapy
It can be done at any age with equal results
advancedTest.explain: Endoscopy trades blood loss and stay for helmet commitment; cognitive superiority is unproven.

advancedTest.q: In a child with Crouzon syndrome and new papilledema after earlier surgery, the most important concern is:
advancedTest.explain: Syndromic patients can redevelop raised ICP; papilledema signals the need for imaging and often vault expansion.

lessons.title: Spinal Dysraphism

levels.kid:
Very early, before a baby is born, the spinal cord starts as a flat strip that rolls up into a tube, like rolling a sheet of paper into a straw.

Sometimes the bottom of the tube does not close all the way. That is called **spina bifida**. In the most serious kind, part of the spinal cord sits in a little sac on the baby's back. Surgeons close the opening very soon after birth to protect the nerves.

In a hidden kind, the skin is closed, but the cord can be stuck at the bottom, like a kite string caught on a branch. As the child grows, it pulls. Surgeons can free it.
levels.hs:
**Spinal dysraphism** means the spine and spinal cord did not form or close properly during the first weeks of development, when the **neural tube** forms and closes.

**Open dysraphism** has nerve tissue exposed or covered only by a thin membrane.
- **Myelomeningocele** is the main type: spinal cord and nerves bulge in a sac on the back. Children often have leg weakness, need help with bladder and bowel control, and most develop **hydrocephalus**. Nearly all have a **Chiari II malformation**.
- Surgery closes the defect, usually within the first days of life, to prevent infection.

**Closed (occult) dysraphism** is covered by skin. Clues on the lower back include a tuft of hair, a deep dimple above the buttock crease, a fatty lump, a birthmark or a skin tag. Types include **lipomyelomeningocele**, **dermal sinus tracts**, **split cord malformations** and a **tight filum terminale**.
- Many cause **tethered cord syndrome**: the low end of the cord is anchored, so it stretches during growth, causing back and leg pain, changes in walking, foot deformities, scoliosis or new bladder problems.
- Surgery **untethers** the cord.

**Prevention**: enough **folic acid** in the diet before birth greatly lowers the risk, which is why many countries fortify flour.
levels.college:
**Embryology.** Primary neurulation forms the neural tube, which closes around the end of the fourth week; failure at the caudal end causes open defects such as myelomeningocele. **Secondary neurulation** forms the conus medullaris and filum terminale from the caudal cell mass, and errors there produce many closed defects.

**Myelomeningocele (MMC)**:
- The **placode** (unclosed neural tissue) sits in the defect, leaking CSF.
- Neurological level predicts function: thoracic and high lumbar lesions usually mean wheelchair use, while sacral lesions may allow independent walking.
- About four in five children historically needed hydrocephalus treatment.
- **Chiari II** with hindbrain herniation is almost universal.
- **Neurogenic bladder** needs early urology care to protect the kidneys, often with clean intermittent catheterization.
- **Latex allergy** is common, so care is latex-free from birth.
- Postnatal closure: the placode is freed, reconstituted into a tube, and covered with dura, fascia and skin, ideally within 24 to 72 hours.
- After closure, many children develop **hydrocephalus** (closing the leak often unmasks it), so head growth and ventricle size are followed closely.

**Closed dysraphism**:
- **Lipomyelomeningocele**: fat continuous with the cord and subcutaneous tissue.
- **Dermal sinus tract**: an epithelial channel from skin toward the dura, which can lead to meningitis or abscess.
- **Split cord malformation**: two hemicords, type I with a bony or cartilaginous spur in separate dural tubes, type II in one dural tube.
- **Tight filum**: a thick or fatty filum with a low conus.

**Imaging**: spinal ultrasound in early infancy through the unossified posterior elements, MRI afterwards. A conus ending below about L2 is suspicious. A simple dimple inside the gluteal cleft and close to the anus is usually benign.
levels.phd:
**Neural tube closure** requires coordinated cell shape changes: apical constriction at hinge points, convergent extension driven by **planar cell polarity** genes such as VANGL1/2 and CELSR1, and fusion of the neural folds. Mouse genetics has implicated hundreds of genes; in humans, risk is polygenic with environmental modifiers. **Folate** supports one-carbon metabolism for nucleotide synthesis and methylation. Food fortification produced large population drops in neural tube defects, yet a residual **folate-resistant** fraction persists, with interest in inositol and other pathways. Certain metabolic conditions and some antiseizure drugs, notably valproate, raise risk.

**The two-hit model** of MMC injury: the first hit is the primary malformation; the second is ongoing damage to exposed neural tissue from chemical and mechanical trauma and CSF leak. This logic underlies gentle handling of the placode and closure as early as safely possible, and it drives research into ways of shortening that exposure; comparative long-term data on newer approaches are still accumulating. Hydrocephalus and Chiari II are the main drivers of later morbidity, so shunt surveillance and hindbrain assessment remain central.

**Tethered cord physiology.** Animal and intraoperative studies suggest traction reduces cord blood flow and oxidative metabolism, giving a plausible mechanism for progressive deficits. Yet the condition defined by imaging (low conus) and the syndrome defined by symptoms do not match neatly; prophylactic untethering of asymptomatic lipomas remains debated, with long-term series offering conflicting results about whether early surgery beats watchful waiting.
levels.expert:
**The newborn with MMC.** Keep the placode moist and covered with sterile saline-soaked dressings, nurse the baby prone, start antibiotics, avoid latex, and examine carefully: the motor level (hip flexion, knee extension, ankle movement), anal tone, head circumference and fontanelle, and any stridor or apnea from Chiari II. Close within days. Watch the ventricles closely afterwards, because closing the leak often unmasks hydrocephalus. Treat with a shunt or, in selected infants, ETV with choroid plexus cauterization.

**Lifelong care** is the real job. These children need a coordinated clinic: neurosurgery, urology, orthopedics, rehabilitation, nutrition and psychology. Deterioration in a child with MMC has a classic differential, and the order matters:
- **Shunt failure** first, always, because it can present subtly (school decline, worsening hand function, new scoliosis, bladder change).
- **Retethering** at the repair site.
- **Syringomyelia**.
- **Symptomatic Chiari II**.

Every repaired MMC looks tethered on MRI, so the diagnosis of retethering is clinical, supported by objective decline (urodynamics, strength, gait, curve progression).

**Untethering surgery** uses intraoperative neurophysiology: free-running and triggered EMG, motor evoked potentials and, increasingly, **sacral reflex** monitoring (the S2 to S4 reflex arc) to protect sacral roots. In complex lipomas, the goal is total or near-total resection with a well-reconstructed neural tube and a capacious dural sac, which in specialist series lowers retethering. A **dermal sinus** should never be probed or injected; it is excised to the dura and often explored intradurally, because inclusion tumors and infection can lie inside.

**Pitfall**: attributing every new problem to "just spina bifida" and missing a treatable shunt failure.

keyPoints: Spinal dysraphism is faulty formation or closure of the neural tube and spine.
Myelomeningocele is an open defect with exposed neural tissue, closed surgically within days of birth.
Most children with myelomeningocele have hydrocephalus and nearly all have a Chiari II malformation.
Skin clues (hair tuft, high dimple, fatty lump, birthmark) suggest closed dysraphism.
Tethered cord syndrome causes pain, gait change, foot deformity, scoliosis and bladder change during growth.
Folic acid fortification lowers neural tube defect risk; after closure, hydrocephalus often appears and needs a shunt or ETV.

test.q: Myelomeningocele is classified as:
test.explain: Neural tissue is exposed or covered only by a thin membrane.

lessons.title: Chiari Malformations

levels.kid:
At the back of your head, under the brain, there is a hole in the skull where the brain connects to the spinal cord. It is like the neck of a funnel.

In a **Chiari malformation**, the bottom part of the back of the brain, called the **tonsils** (not the ones in your throat!), slips down into that hole. It can squeeze things and block the fluid that flows around the brain.

Some people never notice. Others get headaches at the back of the head when they cough or laugh hard. If it causes problems, a surgeon can make the hole roomier so everything flows again.
levels.hs:
The **foramen magnum** is the large opening in the base of the skull where the brainstem becomes the spinal cord. The **cerebellar tonsils** are the lowest part of the cerebellum and normally sit just above it.

**Chiari I malformation**: the tonsils extend below the foramen magnum, usually defined as 5 mm or more on MRI. It is often found by accident and causes no symptoms. When symptoms happen they include:
- **headache at the back of the head made worse by coughing, sneezing, laughing or straining**
- neck pain, dizziness, balance problems
- swallowing trouble or sleep apnea
- **syringomyelia**: a fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) inside the spinal cord, which can cause numbness, weakness and **scoliosis**

**Chiari II malformation** is a different, more severe condition seen in children with **myelomeningocele**. Part of the cerebellar vermis, the brainstem and the fourth ventricle are pulled down. Infants can have breathing pauses, a high-pitched noisy breath (**stridor**) and feeding problems.

**Chiari III** is very rare: hindbrain tissue herniates through a defect at the back of the skull and neck.

Surgery for symptomatic Chiari I is **posterior fossa decompression**: removing a small piece of skull at the back of the head and often part of the first neck vertebra, sometimes with a dural patch, to restore room and CSF flow.
levels.college:
**Chiari I (CM-I)**: tonsillar descent of 5 mm or more below the basion-opisthion (**McRae**) line, with pointed, peg-like tonsils and crowding of the foramen magnum. Many patients have a small posterior fossa, consistent with a mismatch between bony volume and hindbrain. Descent of 3 to 5 mm is borderline. Imaging findings alone do not define disease: many people with tonsillar ectopia are asymptomatic.

**Symptoms** follow obstruction of CSF flow at the foramen magnum and compression:
- **Tussive occipital headache**: brief, triggered by Valsalva.
- Lower cranial nerve signs: dysphagia, hoarseness, sleep apnea.
- Cerebellar signs: ataxia, nystagmus (classically **downbeat**).
- **Syringomyelia** in a substantial minority, often cervical. Classic syrinx findings are **dissociated sensory loss** in a "cape" distribution (pain and temperature lost, light touch preserved, because crossing spinothalamic fibers in the anterior commissure are damaged first), hand weakness and wasting, and scoliosis, often with an atypical left thoracic curve.

**Workup**: brain and whole-spine MRI, sometimes **cine phase-contrast MRI** for CSF flow, sleep study if apnea is suspected.

**Surgery**: suboccipital craniectomy and C1 laminectomy, with or without **duraplasty**. Bone-only decompression has fewer CSF leaks and less pseudomeningocele; duraplasty may lower reoperation in some groups. Tonsillar shrinkage or resection is used by some surgeons.

**Chiari II (CM-II)** accompanies myelomeningocele: descent of the vermis, brainstem and fourth ventricle, tectal beaking, a small posterior fossa and a low torcula. Symptomatic infants have stridor (vocal cord paralysis), apnea, swallowing difficulty and opisthotonus; this is a leading cause of death in myelomeningocele. **Always check shunt function first**, because shunt failure can cause the same signs.
levels.phd:
**Mechanism debates.** The classic theory for Chiari I is a **small posterior fossa** from underdevelopment of the occipital somites, so a normal-sized hindbrain is crowded downwards. Morphometric studies support reduced posterior fossa volume in many patients, but not all. Other cases are acquired: intracranial hypotension from a CSF leak, lumbar shunts or repeated lumbar punctures cause **acquired tonsillar descent** that can reverse with treatment; raised pressure from tumors or idiopathic intracranial hypertension can push tonsils down. Craniosynostosis, especially lambdoid or multisuture forms, and growth hormone deficiency are also associated.

**Syrinx formation** remains incompletely understood. Older theories (Gardner's "water hammer" from the fourth ventricle, Williams' craniospinal pressure dissociation) gave way to the Oldfield model, in which the tonsils act as a piston during each heartbeat, driving systolic pressure waves into the spinal subarachnoid space and forcing fluid into the cord through perivascular spaces. More recent work emphasizes altered CSF compliance and extracellular fluid accumulation rather than simple flow obstruction.

**Craniocervical instability** can coexist, especially in connective tissue disorders and complex Chiari with a retroflexed odontoid or basilar invagination. The **clivo-axial angle** and pB-C2 line help identify ventral compression that may need occipitocervical fusion or ventral decompression, not just posterior decompression.

**Outcome evidence.** The Park-Reeves Syringomyelia Research Consortium has assembled large multicenter pediatric cohorts showing that syrinx improvement after decompression is common, and that duraplasty versus bone-only decompression involves trade-offs; a randomized comparison is ongoing. Natural history data show many incidental Chiari I patients without syrinx remain stable, supporting observation.
levels.expert:
**Who needs surgery?** The hard part of Chiari I is not the operation; it is selection. A child sent for "Chiari" after an MRI for unrelated headaches often has migraine or tension-type headache plus incidental tonsillar ectopia. Surgery for nonspecific headache gives unpredictable results. Strong indications are:
- classic **Valsalva-triggered occipital headache**
- a **syrinx**, especially if enlarging
- lower cranial nerve or brainstem signs, central sleep apnea
- progressive scoliosis with a syrinx

**Examination clues**: test abdominal reflexes (asymmetry suggests syrinx), look for hand wasting, dissociated sensory loss and atypical scoliosis, check gag and palate, and ask about snoring and witnessed apneas.

**Operative pearls**:
- Remove enough bone (a modest suboccipital craniectomy plus C1 arch); an overly wide craniectomy can let the cerebellum sag (**cerebellar ptosis**) and cause new symptoms.
- Intraoperative ultrasound can judge whether bone and band release alone have restored flow before deciding to open the dura.
- If opening the dura, keep the arachnoid intact where possible and use a watertight graft to reduce **pseudomeningocele** and **aseptic meningitis**.
- Watch the **vertebral artery** laterally at C1.

**Complications**: CSF leak, pseudomeningocele, chemical meningitis, wound infection and, rarely, hydrocephalus unmasked after decompression.

**Chiari II emergencies** in infants: new stridor or apnea in a baby with myelomeningocele triggers immediate shunt evaluation; if the shunt works, decompression is considered urgently, because bilateral vocal cord paralysis can progress quickly and some cases need a tracheostomy.

**Expectations**: syrinx shrinkage typically lags behind; scoliosis may still progress, and surgery for headache relief should be discussed with honest uncertainty.

keyPoints: Chiari I: cerebellar tonsils 5 mm or more below the foramen magnum, often found incidentally.
Classic Chiari I symptom: occipital headache triggered by coughing, sneezing or straining.
Syringomyelia gives cape-like loss of pain and temperature with preserved light touch, plus scoliosis.
Chiari II accompanies myelomeningocele and can cause stridor, apnea and swallowing problems in infants.
Always check shunt function first in a child with Chiari II and new symptoms.
Surgery is posterior fossa decompression (suboccipital craniectomy and C1 laminectomy, with or without duraplasty).

test.q: Chiari I malformation is usually defined as tonsillar descent below the foramen magnum of at least:

test.q: Which headache pattern is classic for symptomatic Chiari I?
choices: Headache only on waking in the forehead
Occipital headache triggered by coughing or straining
One-sided headache with flashing lights only
test.explain: Valsalva raises pressure and transiently worsens the block at the foramen magnum.

test.q: A fluid-filled cavity inside the spinal cord is called a:
test.explain: Syringomyelia is the condition of having a syrinx.

test.q: Which sensory pattern suggests a cervical syrinx?
choices: Complete loss of all sensation in both feet
Loss of vision in one eye
Loss of pain and temperature in a cape over the shoulders, light touch preserved
test.explain: Crossing spinothalamic fibers in the anterior commissure are hit first, sparing dorsal column touch.

test.q: Chiari II malformation is classically associated with:
test.explain: Chiari II occurs in nearly all children with myelomeningocele.

test.q: An infant with myelomeningocele develops stridor and breathing pauses. What should be checked first?
test.explain: Shunt failure can worsen hindbrain compression and mimic symptomatic Chiari II.

test.q: Surgery for symptomatic Chiari I is posterior ___ decompression.
test.explain: Removing bone at the back of the skull and C1 gives the hindbrain room.

test.q: Name the large opening in the skull base where the brainstem joins the spinal cord.
test.explain: The tonsils normally sit just above it.

test.q: Which spine problem is commonly linked to a Chiari-related syrinx?
test.explain: A syrinx can weaken paraspinal muscles, causing scoliosis, often with an atypical curve.

test.q: Patching the dura during Chiari decompression is called:
test.explain: A graft enlarges the dura; it may help flow but adds CSF leak risk.

test.q: Pain and temperature fibers cross in the anterior white ___ of the spinal cord.
test.explain: A central syrinx damages these crossing fibers first.

test.q: Tonsillar descent that appears after a CSF leak and reverses when the leak is fixed is called:
test.explain: Low pressure sags the brain; treating the leak can reverse it, so decompression would be wrong.

kidTest.q: Where is the hole the brain connects through?
choices: At the bottom back of the skull
kidTest.explain: It is called the foramen magnum.

kidTest.q: In a Chiari malformation, part of the brain:
kidTest.explain: The tonsils at the bottom of the cerebellum slide down.

kidTest.q: The brain's tonsils are:
kidTest.explain: They share a name because of their shape.

kidTest.q: A Chiari headache often gets worse when you:
kidTest.explain: Pushing hard raises pressure.

kidTest.q: A surgeon can make the hole more ___ so fluid flows again.
kidTest.explain: More room means less squeezing.

kidTest.q: Do all people with Chiari need surgery?
kidTest.explain: Many never have symptoms.

advancedTest.q: A 15-year-old has daily frontal headaches and photophobia; MRI shows 6 mm tonsillar ectopia, no syrinx, normal exam. Best approach?
choices: Treat the likely primary headache and observe the Chiari
advancedTest.explain: Nonspecific headache with incidental ectopia does not predict surgical benefit.

advancedTest.q: A patient develops new tonsillar descent and orthostatic headache after a lumbar drain. Decompression would be harmful because:
choices: This is intracranial hypotension; fixing the low pressure is the treatment
advancedTest.explain: Acquired descent from low pressure reverses when the leak is treated; decompression can worsen sagging.

advancedTest.q: The Oldfield piston model proposes that syrinx fluid enters the cord mainly because:
choices: The fourth ventricle drains directly into the central canal in all patients
Tonsils pulse downwards each heartbeat, driving pressure waves into the spinal subarachnoid space
The cord makes extra CSF on its own
advancedTest.explain: Systolic tonsillar motion forces fluid into the cord through perivascular spaces.

advancedTest.q: After a very wide suboccipital craniectomy, new headaches and sagging cerebellum suggest:
choices: Acute stroke in the frontal lobe
advancedTest.explain: Removing too much bone lets the cerebellum sag; modest craniectomies avoid it.

lessons.title: Pediatric Tumors Surgery

levels.kid:
Sometimes cells in a child's brain grow when they should not. That lump is called a **tumor**. Brain tumors in kids are rare, but they are the most common kind of solid tumor in children.

In kids, many tumors grow in the back of the head, near the part of the brain that helps with balance, called the **cerebellum**. A child might have morning headaches, throw up, or walk wobbly.

A brain surgeon carefully takes out as much of the tumor as is safe. Some tumors are cured by surgery alone. Others also need special medicines or radiation. A whole team of doctors helps the child get strong again.
levels.hs:
Brain and spinal cord tumors are the **most common solid tumors in children** and a leading cause of childhood cancer death. Unlike adults, in whom most tumors are above the tentorium, children over infancy often have **posterior fossa** tumors near the cerebellum and fourth ventricle.

Because these tumors can block CSF flow at the fourth ventricle, many children present with **hydrocephalus**: morning headaches, vomiting, sleepiness, and double vision. Cerebellar tumors cause clumsiness and unsteady walking.

Common pediatric tumors:
- **Pilocytic astrocytoma**: slow-growing, often a cyst with a nodule in the cerebellum. Complete removal is often curative.
- **Medulloblastoma**: a fast-growing malignant tumor of the cerebellum, usually in the midline. Treatment is surgery, then radiation to the brain and spine (in older children) and chemotherapy.
- **Ependymoma**: grows in the fourth ventricle; how completely it is removed strongly affects survival.
- **Craniopharyngioma**: near the pituitary and optic nerves, affecting vision, growth and hormones.
- **Diffuse midline glioma** of the pons: cannot be removed surgically and has a very poor outlook; research is intense.

The surgeon's aim is **maximal safe resection**: remove as much as possible without causing new disability, and treat hydrocephalus. After surgery, oncologists and rehabilitation teams continue care.
levels.college:
**Epidemiology and location.** CNS tumors are the most common solid malignancies of childhood. In children beyond infancy, roughly half arise in the posterior fossa; supratentorial tumors dominate in infants and adolescents.

**Key entities**:
- **Pilocytic astrocytoma** (CNS WHO grade 1): cerebellar cyst with enhancing mural nodule. **KIAA1549-BRAF** fusion is common. Gross total resection is usually curative; removing the nodule matters more than the non-enhancing cyst wall.
- **Medulloblastoma** (grade 4): midline cerebellar embryonal tumor that seeds CSF. Now classified into **WNT-activated**, **SHH-activated** (TP53 status matters), and **non-WNT/non-SHH** (groups 3 and 4). WNT has the best prognosis; group 3 with MYC amplification the worst. Staging requires **whole-spine MRI** and **CSF cytology**, typically about two weeks after surgery. Postoperative MRI within about 48 to 72 hours measures residual tumor.
- **Ependymoma**: posterior fossa types PFA and PFB, and supratentorial ZFTA-fusion and YAP1-fusion types. Tumors squeeze through the foramina of Luschka and Magendie, wrapping lower cranial nerves. **Extent of resection** is the strongest modifiable factor; second-look surgery is used for residual tumor.
- **Diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered**: infiltrative pontine tumor; radiation offers temporary benefit; biopsy is done in some centers for molecular trials.
- **Craniopharyngioma**: adamantinomatous type in children, with calcified, cystic suprasellar mass (CTNNB1 mutations).
- **Atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor**: aggressive tumor in infants with SMARCB1 loss.

**Perioperative issues**:
- Hydrocephalus is managed with steroids, an external ventricular drain or ETV before or during resection; many children do not need a permanent shunt after tumor removal.
- **Posterior fossa syndrome (cerebellar mutism)**: delayed-onset loss of speech, emotional lability and hypotonia after midline resections, most often in medulloblastoma, linked to injury of the dentato-thalamo-cortical pathways.
- Craniospinal radiation is avoided or delayed in very young children because of neurocognitive effects.
levels.phd:
**Molecular neuro-oncology rewrote pediatric classification.** The 2021 WHO CNS classification integrates histology with molecular features, and DNA methylation profiling now assigns many tumors to classes with distinct biology. Medulloblastoma illustrates the shift. **WNT** tumors arise from lower rhombic lip progenitors, carry CTNNB1 mutations, and have excellent survival, prompting trials of reduced therapy. Part of their good prognosis may reflect an abnormal, leaky tumor vasculature that lets chemotherapy in. **SHH** tumors come from cerebellar granule neuron precursors; those with germline TP53 variants (Li-Fraumeni) do poorly and face a high risk of radiation-induced second cancers. Groups 3 and 4 are linked to MYC and MYCN, GFI1 enhancer hijacking and other drivers, and single-cell work traces some to unipolar brush cell lineages.

**Ependymoma** shows how epigenetics can matter more than mutations: PFA tumors have few mutations but a CpG island methylator phenotype and loss of H3 K27 trimethylation, often with **EZHIP** overexpression, mirroring the H3 K27M oncohistone in diffuse midline glioma, which inhibits PRC2.

**Targeted therapy** has arrived for low-grade glioma: BRAF V600E-mutant pediatric low-grade glioma responds to combined BRAF and MEK inhibition, approved for this use in recent years, and type II RAF inhibitors are active against BRAF fusions. This raises the question of when surgery should be less aggressive in eloquent locations such as the hypothalamus or optic pathway.

**For diffuse midline glioma**, research spans the H3 K27M vaccine and GD2-directed CAR T cells delivered into the ventricles, which have produced radiographic and clinical responses in early trials, and ONC201 (dordaviprone), a dopamine receptor antagonist and mitochondrial protease activator, which gained US accelerated approval in 2025 for H3 K27M-mutant glioma.
levels.expert:
**Night of admission.** A child with a large posterior fossa mass, obstructive hydrocephalus and vomiting is usually stabilized with dexamethasone; an EVD is reserved for deterioration, because sudden decompression from below can risk **upward herniation** or tumor bleeding. Many teams resect within days, often with the drain placed at surgery, then wean it.

**Operating in the posterior fossa**: the child is usually prone with the neck flexed and head fixed (pin fixation is modified or avoided in very young children because the skull is thin). Approaches:
- **Telovelar approach**: open the tela choroidea and inferior medullary velum instead of splitting the vermis, which may reduce posterior fossa syndrome risk.
- Respect the floor of the fourth ventricle: the facial colliculus and the nuclei of cranial nerves VI, VII, IX, X and XII are millimeters deep. Neuromonitoring with direct stimulation of the floor helps map them.
- In ependymoma, follow tumor out through the foramen of Luschka into the cerebellopontine angle while protecting lower cranial nerves.

**Extent of resection is a judgment call** by tumor type. For ependymoma, gross total resection is the goal and a second-look operation is common. For medulloblastoma, small residual disease matters less in the molecular era, so leaving a sliver on the brainstem is better than a deficit. For **craniopharyngioma**, the old goal of radical resection caused hypothalamic obesity and memory loss; many centers now favor **hypothalamus-sparing** subtotal resection plus proton radiotherapy or cyst drainage.

**After surgery**: watch for mutism, swallowing problems, CSF leak and pseudomeningocele, and hydrocephalus needing a shunt or ETV. Coordinate with oncology, endocrinology, ophthalmology and neuropsychology. Long-term survivors face hearing loss, growth and hormone problems, and learning difficulties, so survivorship clinics are part of the operation's real outcome.

keyPoints: CNS tumors are the most common solid tumors of childhood; many occur in the posterior fossa.
Posterior fossa tumors often present with hydrocephalus (morning headache, vomiting) and ataxia.
Pilocytic astrocytoma (cyst with mural nodule) is often cured by complete resection.
Medulloblastoma has molecular groups (WNT, SHH, group 3, group 4); WNT has the best prognosis.
Extent of resection strongly affects ependymoma survival.
Posterior fossa syndrome (cerebellar mutism) can follow midline resections.

test.q: Brain and spinal cord tumors in children are:
choices: Less common than all other solid tumors
The most common solid tumors of childhood
test.explain: CNS tumors are the most common solid malignancies in children.

test.q: Why do many posterior fossa tumors cause morning headache and vomiting?
choices: They block CSF flow and cause hydrocephalus
test.explain: Fourth ventricle obstruction raises pressure, often worst after lying flat overnight.

test.q: A cerebellar cyst with an enhancing mural nodule in a child most likely is:
test.explain: This classic look plus a BRAF fusion fits pilocytic astrocytoma.

test.q: Which medulloblastoma group has the best prognosis?
test.explain: WNT tumors have excellent survival, leading to trials of reduced therapy.

test.q: Why is the whole spine imaged in medulloblastoma?
choices: It always starts in the spine
It can seed through the CSF
test.explain: CSF dissemination changes staging and treatment.

test.q: For ependymoma, the strongest modifiable factor for survival is:
choices: The time of day of surgery
test.explain: Gross total resection is linked to better survival, so second-look surgery is used for residual tumor.

test.q: What is the delayed loss of speech after midline posterior fossa surgery called? (two words)
test.explain: Also called posterior fossa syndrome, linked to dentato-thalamo-cortical injury.

test.q: The surgical goal of removing as much tumor as possible without new deficits is called maximal ___ resection.
test.explain: Maximal safe resection balances cure and function.

test.q: A suprasellar, calcified, cystic tumor in a child with poor vision and slow growth is most likely:
test.explain: Craniopharyngiomas sit near the pituitary and optic chiasm.

test.q: Diffuse midline glioma of the pons is usually treated with:
test.explain: It infiltrates the brainstem, so resection is not possible; radiation gives temporary benefit.

test.q: Pilocytic astrocytomas commonly carry a KIAA1549-___ fusion.
test.explain: This fusion activates MAPK signaling.

test.q: Why is craniospinal radiation avoided or delayed in very young children?
choices: It can seriously harm brain development
It does not kill tumor cells
test.explain: Neurocognitive and growth effects are greatest in young children.

kidTest.q: A tumor is:
choices: A lump of cells growing when they should not
kidTest.explain: Cells grow too much and form a lump.

kidTest.q: Many kids' brain tumors grow:
choices: In the back of the head
kidTest.explain: Near the cerebellum.

kidTest.q: The cerebellum helps with:
kidTest.explain: It helps you walk steadily.

kidTest.q: A child with a brain tumor might have:
kidTest.explain: Extra pressure causes these signs.

kidTest.q: A brain surgeon takes out as much of the tumor as is ___.
kidTest.explain: Safety comes first.

kidTest.q: Who helps a child after brain surgery?
choices: A whole team of doctors and helpers
kidTest.explain: Many experts help the child recover.

advancedTest.q: A child with a midline cerebellar tumor and hydrocephalus is stable on steroids. Why might a team avoid placing an EVD immediately before resection?
choices: Rapid decompression from above risks upward herniation or tumor bleeding
advancedTest.explain: Supratentorial drainage with a full posterior fossa can provoke upward transtentorial herniation.

advancedTest.q: Loss of H3 K27 trimethylation is shared by diffuse midline glioma and which tumor?
advancedTest.explain: PFA ependymomas often overexpress EZHIP, which inhibits PRC2 much like H3 K27M does.

advancedTest.q: For childhood craniopharyngioma, why do many centers now favor hypothalamus-sparing subtotal resection plus radiation?
choices: Radical resection often caused hypothalamic obesity and memory problems
The tumor is always benign and never recurs
advancedTest.explain: Quality of life after hypothalamic injury drove the shift to less aggressive surgery.

advancedTest.q: The telovelar approach to the fourth ventricle is preferred over vermian splitting mainly to:
choices: Reduce injury linked to cerebellar mutism
advancedTest.explain: Opening the tela choroidea and inferior velum spares the vermis and possibly the dentate pathways.
